Cloudflare DNS Problems and How to Fix Them

By WevTEC Review TeamPublished Jul 17, 2025Updated Oct 25, 202610 min read
On This Page
  1. The short answer
  2. Orange vs grey cloud
  3. Domain not resolving
  4. Email stopped working
  5. SSL errors and redirect loops
  6. 520, 521 and 403 errors
  7. Changes not taking effect
  8. Questions people ask AI
  9. How WevTEC Fix Website Issues helps

Site or email still broken? Book a free consultation

Cloudflare is doing useful work for a large share of the web: DNS, caching, SSL and DDoS protection. It is also one of the easiest places to take your own site — or your email — offline with a single setting.

These are the Cloudflare DNS problems that come up most often, what causes each one, and how to fix them without disabling the protection you set Cloudflare up for in the first place.

The short answer

Most Cloudflare problems trace back to one setting: whether a DNS record is proxied (orange cloud) or DNS only (grey cloud). Cloudflare forwards web traffic only, so proxying a mail or FTP record breaks it.

If email stopped working, set your mail records to grey cloud. If you get endless redirects, your SSL mode is probably Flexible while your server forces HTTPS — install a certificate at the origin and switch to Full (strict). If you see 520, 521 or 522, Cloudflare reached your server and your server is the problem.

If the site will not resolve at all, check that your registrar is actually using Cloudflare’s nameservers before changing anything else.

The orange cloud explains most Cloudflare problems

Cloudflare sits between your visitors and your server. Each DNS record you create carries a proxy status, shown as an orange or grey cloud, and that single setting explains a large share of the problems people run into.

Orange cloud (proxied) means traffic for that record goes through Cloudflare first. You get caching, the firewall and DDoS protection, and your server’s real IP address is hidden. Grey cloud (DNS only) means Cloudflare answers the DNS lookup and then steps aside; traffic goes straight to your server.

Proxying only works for HTTP and HTTPS traffic. Cloudflare’s own documentation on proxy status is explicit about this. Anything that is not web traffic — mail delivery on port 25, IMAP, SMTP, FTP, SSH, a database connection — breaks the moment you proxy it, because Cloudflare will not forward those ports.

So before troubleshooting anything else, look at the cloud icons. Web records (@ and www) generally want orange. Mail and service records (mail, webmail, ftp, cpanel) must be grey.

The domain will not resolve at all

A browser showing DNS_PROBE_FINISHED_NXDOMAIN or “site can’t be reached” means the name did not resolve to an address at all. Three things cause nearly all of it.

The nameservers are not pointed at Cloudflare. Cloudflare only controls your DNS once your registrar — GoDaddy, Namecheap, whoever you bought the domain from — is using the two Cloudflare nameservers it assigned you. In the Cloudflare dashboard, the site will show as “Pending Nameserver Update” until this is done. Check the registrar, not Cloudflare.

The A record is missing or wrong. You need an A record for @ pointing at your server’s IP address, and usually a CNAME for www pointing at your root domain. If you moved hosts and forgot to update the IP, the name resolves to a server that no longer hosts you.

The domain itself has lapsed. An expired or suspended domain will not resolve regardless of what Cloudflare says. Check the expiry date at your registrar before assuming the DNS is at fault.

One caution: if you have just changed nameservers, give it time. Registrar changes commonly take a few hours to be seen everywhere, and testing from a single computer with a cached result will mislead you.

Email stopped working after you enabled Cloudflare

This is the most frequent Cloudflare problem we see, and it is almost always the orange cloud.

Mail does not travel over HTTP. If the A record your mail server uses — usually mail.yourdomain.com — is proxied, Cloudflare will not pass the mail ports through, and sending or receiving stops. Set that record to grey cloud (DNS only) and mail generally starts working again within minutes.

Two other things to check:

  • MX records survived the move. When Cloudflare imports your existing DNS it usually picks up MX records, but not always, and anything it missed has to be added by hand. Get the correct values from your mail provider — Google Workspace, Microsoft 365 and cPanel each publish theirs — rather than guessing.
  • SPF, DKIM and DMARC came across. These are TXT records. If they were left behind, your mail will still send but a growing share of it will land in spam folders. That symptom often shows up days later and gets blamed on something else.

If mail is routed to the same server as your website, the host whose A record you proxy still matters: keep the web name orange and the mail name grey, even though both point at the same IP.

SSL errors and redirect loops

SSL errors and infinite redirect loops after enabling Cloudflare nearly always come down to the encryption mode, found under SSL/TLS in the dashboard. Cloudflare documents four modes, and the difference matters:

  • Full (strict) encrypts both legs and validates the certificate on your server. This is what you want.
  • Full encrypts both legs but accepts a self-signed certificate on your server.
  • Flexible encrypts only between the visitor and Cloudflare. The connection from Cloudflare to your server is plain HTTP.
  • Off disables encryption entirely.

Flexible mode is the usual cause of redirect loops. Cloudflare requests your site over HTTP; your server is configured to force HTTPS, so it redirects; Cloudflare requests again over HTTP; the loop never ends. The browser gives up with ERR_TOO_MANY_REDIRECTS.

The fix is to install a real certificate on your origin server and switch to Full (strict). Most hosts now issue free Let’s Encrypt certificates, and Cloudflare also offers a free Origin CA certificate. Treat Flexible as a temporary measure at best: visitors see a padlock while part of the journey is unencrypted, which is misleading, and on a site handling logins or payments it is a real risk.

If you see ERR_SSL_VERSION_OR_CIPHER_MISMATCH, the certificate covering your hostname is usually missing or expired at the origin. Our guide to fixing a site marked Not Secure walks through that side of it.

520, 521, 522 and 403 errors

These errors come from Cloudflare itself, which is useful: they tell you Cloudflare reached your server and did not like what came back. Cloudflare’s reference for 5xx errors lists them all; three account for most cases.

521 — Web server is down. Your server actively refused the connection. Either it genuinely is down, or its firewall is blocking Cloudflare. This is common after enabling a security plugin or a server firewall that does not know Cloudflare’s address ranges. Allow Cloudflare’s published IP ranges at the server.

522 — Connection timed out. Your server accepted the connection and then never answered. Usually overload: exhausted PHP workers, a database locked under load, or a runaway process. The fix is on the server, not in Cloudflare.

520 — Unknown error. The catch-all. Your server returned something malformed, such as an empty response or oversized headers. Check your server’s error log at the time of failure; this is one case where the log usually names the cause outright.

A 403 Forbidden is different. It generally comes from a rule rather than a fault: a Cloudflare firewall rule, a rate limit, a country block, or a WAF rule catching legitimate traffic. The Security Events screen shows exactly which rule fired, which beats guessing. If your own address is being caught, our guide to checking and unblocking an IP covers the server side.

Changes that seem to do nothing

“I changed it and nothing happened” usually has a simpler explanation than DNS propagation.

Cloudflare is caching the old version. DNS changes take effect quickly, but cached HTML and assets do not. Purge the cache from the Caching screen, and use Development Mode while you are actively making changes — it bypasses the cache for three hours.

Your browser is caching. Test in a private window, or from your phone on mobile data. This alone resolves a surprising share of reported DNS problems.

Another DNS layer is in the way. If your registrar, your host and Cloudflare all hold records, only the nameservers you actually delegated to are being used. Editing records in the wrong place changes nothing at all — a common waste of an afternoon.

When you need to know what the world sees rather than what your computer sees, query a public resolver directly or use an external DNS lookup tool. Checking from the machine that just made the change is the least reliable test available.

Not sure which layer is broken?

DNS problems are hard to diagnose from the outside, which is exactly why they drag on. Send us the domain and the symptom and we will tell you where the fault actually sits — registrar, Cloudflare, or your server.

Questions people ask AI about Cloudflare DNS

“Why did my email stop working after I set up Cloudflare?”

Almost always because a mail record is proxied. Cloudflare only forwards HTTP and HTTPS traffic, so a mail host set to the orange cloud blocks SMTP and IMAP. Set mail, webmail and similar records to grey cloud (DNS only), and confirm your MX and SPF records made it across.

“What is the difference between the orange and grey cloud?”

Orange means traffic for that record passes through Cloudflare, giving you caching, firewall and DDoS protection while hiding your server IP. Grey means Cloudflare answers the DNS lookup only and traffic goes straight to your server. Web records want orange; mail and FTP records must be grey.

“Why does my site show too many redirects after enabling Cloudflare?”

Usually the SSL mode is set to Flexible while your server forces HTTPS. Cloudflare requests over HTTP, your server redirects to HTTPS, and the loop repeats. Install a certificate on your server and switch to Full (strict).

“How long do Cloudflare DNS changes take to work?”

Record changes within Cloudflare are usually live in under a minute. Changing nameservers at your registrar is the slow part and can take several hours to be seen everywhere. If a change seems to do nothing, check your browser cache and whether you edited records in the right place first.

“What does Cloudflare error 521 mean?”

Your server refused the connection. Either it is down, or its firewall is blocking Cloudflare. Allowing Cloudflare’s published IP ranges at the server fixes most cases. A 522 is different: the server accepted the connection and then never replied, which usually means overload.

“Is Flexible SSL mode safe to use?”

Not as a permanent setting. It encrypts the visitor-to-Cloudflare leg but leaves Cloudflare-to-server unencrypted, so visitors see a padlock that overstates how protected they are. On any site with logins or payments, install a certificate at the origin and use Full (strict).

That ordering matters, because editing records in the wrong layer is the most common way an outage gets longer instead of shorter.
